passed.title: pct_change returns a fraction and gives inf after a zero, not null
passed.trap: `Series.pct_change` returns the change as a fraction (0.5 means +50%), not a percentage, so multiply by 100 yourself if you need percent. When the earlier value is 0, the result is `inf`, not null or an error, and that `inf` silently poisons later means and sums. Guard zero denominators explicitly, for example with `pl.when` on the shifted value, before you aggregate.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("price", [0.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0])
print(s.pct_change().to_list())
print(s.pct_change().mean())

safe = s.to_frame().select(
    pl.when(pl.col("price").shift() == 0)
    .then(None)
    .otherwise(pl.col("price").pct_change() * 100)
    .alias("pct")
)
print(safe["pct"].to_list())
print(safe["pct"].mean())

passed.title: Integer pow keeps the integer dtype; use a float exponent for roots and negative powers
passed.trap: `Series.pow` follows the dtype of the base unless the exponent is a float. An integer Series raised to an integer exponent stays integer. To raise integers to a negative power, the docstring says to cast the base or the exponent to float, for example pass `-1.0` instead of `-1`. A float exponent makes the result follow the exponent's float dtype.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("x", [1, 2, 3, 4])
sq = s.pow(2)
print(sq.dtype, sq.to_list())

root = s.pow(0.5)
print(root.dtype, root.to_list())

inv = s.pow(-1.0)
print(inv.dtype, inv.to_list())

passed.title: Rolling skew, kurtosis and map default min_samples to the full window
passed.trap: For `Series.rolling_map`, `Series.rolling_skew` and `Series.rolling_kurtosis`, `min_samples=None` means `min_samples = window_size`. The first `window_size - 1` results are therefore null. Pass `min_samples` explicitly if you want partial windows. In `Series.rolling_map` the old `min_periods` parameter was renamed to `min_samples` in 1.21.0, so use the new name. These three methods are also marked unstable.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("v", [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
print(s.rolling_map(lambda w: w.sum(), window_size=3).to_list())
print(s.rolling_map(lambda w: w.sum(), window_size=3, min_samples=1).to_list())

passed.title: Series.std defaults to the sample standard deviation (ddof=1), unlike NumPy
passed.trap: `Series.std` divides by N - 1 by default (`ddof=1`). This matches pandas, but code ported from NumPy (`np.std` uses ddof=0) will get different numbers. Pass `ddof=0` when you need the population standard deviation.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3])
print(s.std())
print(s.std(ddof=0))

passed.title: rle_id numbers runs of consecutive values, not distinct values
passed.trap: `Series.rle_id` starts a new ID every time the value changes. A value that reappears later gets a new ID, so it is not a distinct-value ID or a categorical code. A null also forms its own run. `Series.rle` likewise returns one row per run, not one row per unique value. Use these methods to group consecutive streaks; to count distinct values, use `Series.n_unique` or `Series.value_counts`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("state", ["a", "a", "b", "a", None, "a"])
print(s.rle_id().to_list())
print(s.rle_id().max() + 1, s.n_unique())
print(s.rle().struct.unnest())

passed.title: Series.set takes a boolean mask, Series.scatter takes positions; both are anti-patterns
passed.trap: pandas users reach for `.loc` or `.iloc` style assignment. In Polars, `Series.set` expects a boolean mask the same length as the Series, while `Series.scatter` expects integer index positions; mixing them up gives wrong rows or an error. The docstrings call both an anti-pattern that can block optimization such as predicate pushdown. Prefer `pl.when(predicate).then(value).otherwise(...)` inside `DataFrame.select` or `DataFrame.with_columns`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s1 = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3])
print(s1.set(s1 == 2, 10).to_list())

s2 = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3])
print(s2.scatter([0], [99]).to_list())

out = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3]).to_frame().select(
    pl.when(pl.col("a") == 2).then(10).otherwise(pl.col("a")).alias("a")
)
print(out["a"].to_list())
